query: Earlier W-based high-entropy alloys showed promising microstructural stability, high-temperature strength, and irradiation tolerance, but most contained Nb, Mo, Cr, or Ni, whose activation behavior and other service limitations restrict their suitability for plasma-facing components. Candidate structural materials must combine thermal and mechanical performance with low neutron activation and rapid radioactive decay. The equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy uses refractory, relatively low-activation constituents and has shown creep and molten-salt-corrosion resistance, yet its plastic strain and toughness remain unreported and poorly understood. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to pure tungsten, the boundaries of validity, the cited prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare the plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy to pure tungsten under high-temperature plasma-facing-component service conditions, using a combination of experimental and simulation approaches
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the plastic strain and toughness of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy are not significantly improved compared to pure tungsten, or if the solid-solution strengthening mechanism is not observed, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Previous studies on (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys have already demonstrated notable mechanical properties as candidates for the thermal barrier interlayer []; for example, showing a ductile behavior strain–-stress magnitude of around 300 MPa for vanadium and around 400 MPa for chromium-based alloys, exhibited at 1000 °C. Nevertheless, there is still a lack of knowledge on thermal stability at higher temperatures and irradiation resistance, which are important aspects to consider for the behavior of the materials subject to extreme environments, especially nuclear fusion. Refractory, low activation high-entropy alloys such as TiVCrTa [], TiVCrFeMn [], and (CrVTiTa)1−xWx [], where x is the atomic fraction (0.3 to 0.9), have been proposed for nuclear applications. This class of alloys is particularly promising as a thermal barrier interlayer due to its high thermal stability [] and high temperature strength [,], as well as high radiation resistance [] and low thermal diffusivity []. Based on this, the study of refractory alloys was pursued based on W, since it is the chosen plasma-facing component. This work presents the production of entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys

The requirement of innovative plasma-facing and high-temperature materials has turned researchers’ attention towards refractory metals due to their high-temperature properties, such as a high melting temperature, good strength, and good creep resistance. Intensive research has explored the properties and performance of tungsten in plasma-facing applications, , . A unique combination of various physical, chemical, mechanical and irradiation characteristics, including a high melting temperature, good thermal conductivity, a proper sputtering threshold, , good creep strength, a low level of tritium retention, and neutron activation and erosion have made W a potential material for plasma-facing components of fusion reactors, . Although the potential of W for use as a plasma-facing material is accepted, its commercial roles remain restricted due to its high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT), radiation-induced embrittlement, its low yield strength and the fact that it oxidizes readily at elevated temperatures into WO3, which is volatile above ~1000 °C, , , . Mitigation of these deficiencies is essential, . Therefore, extensive research is being done to explore new W alloys

Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels.
